title: The Result You Meant to Keep: Writing a File That Is Whole or Not There

questions.question: A program opens a stream on a path in a folder that does not exist, writes a line, and carries on. What happens?
options: The line is written to the nearest folder that does exist
An exception is thrown at the line that opened the stream
The folder is created, because opening for writing creates what is missing
Nothing visible: no exception, the stream sets a failure flag, and every write is silently dropped
questions.explanation: Measured: no exception, is_open false, good false after the write. The program exits with status 0 having saved nothing, which is why the stream has to be checked.

questions.question: A 27 byte calibration file is opened with std::ofstream for writing, and the program is stopped before it writes anything. How big is the file?
options: 27 bytes, since nothing was written
0 bytes, because opening for writing empties the file at the open
It depends on whether the stream was flushed
27 bytes, but marked as unreadable
questions.explanation: Measured: 0 bytes the moment the stream existed. From that line until the last byte is written there is no old file and no new one, which is why the new contents are written beside the old file instead.

questions.question: A program writes 1000 rows, 7000 bytes, through a stream and then calls abort(). How much is on disk afterwards, and what changes it?
options: 0 bytes with plain writes and 7000 with std::endl after each row, because the rows were waiting in the stream's buffer
All 7000 bytes, since write calls go straight to the disk
Half of them, because the buffer is flushed when it is half full
0 bytes however it is written, because abort discards everything
questions.explanation: The buffer belongs to the process and dies with it. endl flushes after each row, which is right for a log that must survive a crash and costs a write per row. It does nothing for a file that must be replaced whole.

questions.question: A ten row log of 0.5,1.5 is cut off after 77 bytes and read back with lesson 01-12's reader. What does the reader report?
options: One row of the wrong width, since the last row is short
Nine rows and one unparsable line
Ten rows, nothing rejected, and a last value of 1 where the logger meant 1.5
An error, since the file does not end in a newline
questions.explanation: The last row was cut after 0.5,1, which is the right width and a good number. A reader cannot tell a short number from a number that is short, so a file that stops partway can be a valid file, and the only protection is to never leave one.

questions.question: Why does save_text write to a temporary file and rename it, instead of writing the destination directly?
options: Because std::ofstream cannot open an existing file
Renaming is faster than writing
So the old file is untouched until the new one is complete, and a reader sees the old file or the new one and never half of either
So the file can be written by two programs at once
questions.explanation: The destination is only changed by the rename, which replaces it in one step on Linux and Windows. A failure before that point leaves the old file exactly as it was. It does not make two writers safe, since they would share the temporary name.

questions.question: Why does exact_text start at 15 digits and widen, rather than always writing 17?
options: Seventeen is always correct but writes 0.1 as 0.10000000000000001
Fifteen is the most a stream will print
Seventeen digits is not enough for every double
Because 17 digits is slower to write than 15
questions.explanation: It starts at the 15 digits any typed decimal survives and widens only if the value does not read back. digits10 is 15, so a decimal that long survives being a double. max_digits10 is 17, so a double that long survives being a decimal. Trying 15, 16, 17 gives the shortest text that reads back identically: 2.45 stays 2.45 and 0.1 + 0.2 becomes 0.30000000000000004.
